additions.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 as regards the simplification of certain sustainability reporting standards
additions.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Official Journal of the European Union)
additions.locator: Annex, ESRS 1 General Requirements, chapter 5, paragraphs 62 to 66; Article 3 (entry into force and application)
additions.quote: does not require information on each and every actor in the upstream and downstream value chain but only the inclusion of material information
additions.why: The reporting standard an EU customer in scope will follow from financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. It tells the customer what it must gather from its value chain: material information only, which may come from suppliers directly or from estimates (paragraph 65), and paragraph 66 ties requests to protected undertakings to the Annex II datapoints of Regulation (EU) 2026/1560. This is the text a supplier's map of customer duties should be drawn from. Enters into force on 10 November 2026, so not yet in force on the day it was read. Official Journal text served by the Publications Office because EUR-Lex returned empty pages.

additions.title: UK SRS S1: General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information
additions.locator: Appendix A, defined term 'value chain' (printed page 21, PDF page 25); paragraph 2 (PDF page 7); Appendix B, paragraph B5 (printed page 23, PDF page 27)
additions.quote: The full range of interactions, resources and relationships related to a reporting entity's business model and the external environment in which it operates.
additions.why: The UK general standard that listed customers will report against under the Financial Conduct Authority's rules. Its definition of the value chain is the reason a UK reporting customer looks to its suppliers: supply and distribution channels are named in paragraph B5. Voluntary unless another rule requires it; an investor-focused standard based on IFRS S1, not written for small firms. The existing list has the climate standard (S2) under a different criterion; this is the general standard.

additions.title: Supervisory statement 5/25: Enhancing banks' and insurers' approaches to managing climate-related risks
additions.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
additions.locator: Paragraphs 4.25 to 4.31 (printed pages 17 to 18, PDF pages 19 to 20); chapter 1, 'Scope' (printed page 4); commencement at paragraph 3.1
additions.quote: firms should seek to obtain this information where possible (eg during client onboarding or annual reviews)
additions.why: The UK source for the finance column of the map. The prudential regulator expects banks and insurers to understand climate risk in their material client relationships and, where they lack the information, to seek it from clients at onboarding or annual review, or to use public data or proxies. This is the first UK regulator text found on why lenders ask borrowers for climate data; the earlier pass could read no lender source. Supervisory expectations addressed to banks and insurers, applied proportionately; they place no duty on the client. Commenced 3 December 2025 and replaced SS3/19.

additions.title: Scope 3 Emissions in the UK Reporting Landscape: Call for Evidence Analysis Report
additions.publisher: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
additions.locator: Chapter 2, 'SME Impacts', PDF page 18; introduction, PDF page 6 (184 responses)
additions.quote: they possibly may be obliged to provide data to larger organisations, if they are a supplier to larger reporting firms
additions.why: UK government evidence that value-chain reporting reaches firms outside its scope. In the analysis of responses to the 2023 call for evidence, concern about the cost and resource impact on small and medium-sized firms was raised 45 times. Dated May 2024 on the cover. A thematic analysis of 184 self-selected consultation responses, not a survey and not government policy; it predates the UK Sustainability Reporting Standards and the 2026 listing rules.

additions.title: SMEs and Net Zero 2025: UK Net Zero Business Census report
additions.locator: 'Tracking and measuring carbon emissions', page 17; summary table, page 16; Appendix I (survey sample and methodology), page 48
additions.quote: Nearly 1 in 10 SMEs (9%) have been asked to report carbon footprint data by customers or when tendering in the last 12 months
additions.why: A UK figure for how often requests actually arrive, which the brief lacks: 9% of smaller businesses overall, rising from 3% of those with no employees to 37% of medium-sized ones. Construction and utilities are the sectors most often asked. Based on 1,783 smaller businesses surveyed in the 2025 UK Net Zero Business Census; publication date printed as October 2025. A survey report by the government-owned development bank, not peer reviewed; it covers carbon data only, not wider sustainability requests. The bank's site refused automated reading on 2 October 2026 and answered on 5 October 2026.

additions.title: Data Requests in Value Chains: The Effects of Corporate Sustainability Reporting on SMEs in The Netherlands
additions.publisher: Niemann, Morssinkhof, van der Linden and de Vries, Sustainability 17(17), 8029 (MDPI); copy held in the Delft University of Technology repository
additions.locator: Abstract (article page 1, PDF page 2); section 3.1 and Figure 1 (article page 5, PDF page 6)
additions.quote: A key finding is that most Dutch SMEs (72%) have not yet received sustainability data requests.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed evidence on how far reporting duties have reached suppliers so far. A survey of 431 Dutch small and medium-sized firms and 48 interviews in late 2024: 72% had received no request, but exposure rose sharply with size and with international value chains, and requests centred on carbon emissions and material use. Supports mapping customers by size and reach instead of assuming every customer will ask. Dutch sample, 19% response rate, fieldwork before the 2026 directive narrowed scope. Read in the university repository's copy of the final published version because the journal's own site refused automated reading.

additions.title: Dear supplier, how sustainable are you? A multiple-case study analysis of a widespread tool for sustainable supply chain management
additions.publisher: Fraser and co-authors, Sustainability Management Forum 28, 127-149 (Springer)
additions.quote: Social desirability bias and supplier assessment fatigue were identified as issues confronting such questionnaires.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed study of the supplier questionnaire, the instrument by which a customer's duty usually arrives. It finds that suppliers tire of repeated assessments and tend to give the answers they think are wanted, which is the research basis for the brief's point that a firm caught by surprise answers with guesses. A multiple-case study, so the findings are not statistically generalisable; published in 2020, before the EU and UK rules now in force. Open access on the publisher's site.

additions.title: Fostering convergence in SME sustainability reporting (OECD SME and Entrepreneurship Papers)
additions.locator: Section 1 (printed page 10, PDF page 11); executive summary (printed page 6, PDF page 7)
additions.quote: Thus, despite technically being exempt from such reporting, SMEs are impacted by this "trickle-down" effect of reporting demands.
additions.why: International comparator. The OECD finds the same pattern across jurisdictions: large companies and financial institutions pass their reporting needs to small suppliers and borrowers, in the absence of a common framework. Shows the position is not peculiar to the EU or the UK. A policy paper approved by the OECD Committee on SMEs and Entrepreneurship on 20 January 2025; it describes the EU voluntary standard while still a draft and predates the 2026 directive.

rejected.title: UK Net Zero Business Census 2024: results and recommendations
rejected.reason: Fetched. Superseded for this purpose by the British Business Bank report on the 2025 census, which has the more recent figures. Not added, to avoid padding.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. Two refinements: (1) the brief says no UK law was found that limits what a customer may ask; for public buyers only, the Procurement Act 2023 (sections 12(4) and 22) requires regard to barriers facing small firms and proportionate conditions of participation, so the sentence holds for private customers but is too wide for public ones. (2) The brief has no UK figure for how often requests arrive; the British Business Bank reports 9% of smaller businesses, 37% of medium-sized ones (page 17). The PRA's SS5/25 now supplies the lender source the first pass could not read.
